meta.title: Autumn Budget 2026
meta.statusNote: The speech is over. The OBR has published its forecasts, and its press conference is at 14:30. We're working through the full Budget documents.

measures.headline: £100 Household Energy Payment this winter
measures.detail: About 20 million households in council tax bands A to D will get £100 paid straight into their bank accounts this winter. It costs £2.6bn. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland get funding and are being urged to pass it on.
measures.impact: If your home is in council tax band A, B, C or D in England, expect £100 towards energy bills over winter. Elsewhere in the UK, it depends on your devolved government. Campaigners say it will 'barely dent' bills: the price cap is now £1,723, and a rise of around 22% is forecast for January.

measures.headline: Standing charges on gas bills scrapped
measures.detail: Confirmed in the speech: Ofgem will remove the fixed daily standing charge from household gas bills from next year. Similar reforms are planned for electricity.
measures.impact: The charge is about £108 a year now, but the cost is expected to move into the price per unit of gas. Martin Lewis estimates around 60% of households will pay less, mostly low users, and 40% will pay more. Reports put typical savings at roughly £22 to £50 a year.

measures.headline: Cash ISA limit stays at £20,000
measures.detail: Confirmed in the speech: the plan to cut the cash ISA limit is reversed, so it stays at £20,000 a year tax-free. Healey says 88% of people will pay no more tax on savings. A new 'Starter ISA' for first-time investors is being worked up with the industry.
measures.impact: Nothing changes. You can still put up to £20,000 a year into ISAs tax-free, all in cash if you like.

measures.headline: No rise in income tax, employee NI or VAT rates
measures.detail: Confirmed in the speech: no rises in the rates of income tax, employee National Insurance or VAT, and no tax rises on wages or dividends. Extra revenue comes mainly from the banks and from tougher tax collection.
measures.impact: The rates on your payslip and on most shopping won't go up. Taxes can still rise in other ways, though, for example by keeping thresholds frozen.

measures.headline: No rise in the £12,570 tax-free allowance announced
measures.detail: Despite calls to end the freeze, the speech made no change to the personal allowance. It stays at £12,570, frozen since 2021 and currently set to stay there until 2031. The IFS estimated unfreezing it would cost around £6.7bn to £8.4bn a year. The only change is for pensioners living on the State Pension alone, who won't pay income tax.
measures.impact: As wages rise, more of your pay keeps getting taxed (fiscal drag). We'll confirm against the full Budget documents when they're published.

measures.headline: VAT cut on electricity extended to July
measures.detail: The existing VAT cut on household electricity, covering 29 million households, is extended through winter and spring until July.
measures.impact: Worth about £50 off the annual energy price cap for a typical household.

measures.headline: Higher tax-free mileage rate
measures.detail: The tax-free rate for using your own car for work becomes a permanent 55p a mile for the first 10,000 miles. Beyond that it goes up from 25p to 35p a mile.
measures.impact: If you drive your own car for work, you can be paid more per mile without paying tax on it.

measures.headline: Import tariffs scrapped on 100+ supermarket items
measures.detail: Tariffs are being removed on more than 100 everyday products sold in supermarkets.
measures.impact: Estimated to save the average family about £21 a year on food shopping, if shops pass it on.

measures.headline: Paternity pay for the self-employed
measures.detail: Self-employed new parents can get up to two weeks of statutory paternity pay, worth up to £194 a week.
measures.impact: Self-employed dads and partners can take time off after a birth without losing all their income.

measures.headline: No income tax on a full State Pension
measures.detail: A new Pension Tax Allowance means pensioners whose income is no more than the full new State Pension won't pay income tax for the rest of this Parliament. Separately, ex-miners get every penny of their pension fund surplus.
measures.impact: Pensioners living on just the State Pension won't be dragged into income tax as the pension rises.

measures.headline: Minimum wage up 3.9%
measures.detail: Both the National Minimum Wage and the National Living Wage rise by 3.9%, covering 2.3 million of the lowest-paid workers.
measures.impact: A pay rise for the lowest-paid, normally from April. For a full-time worker it's roughly in line with inflation.

measures.headline: Carer's Allowance 'cliff edge' replaced with a taper
measures.detail: Instead of losing all of Carer's Allowance for earning £1 over the weekly limit, carers will lose £1 of support for every £1 they earn above it.
measures.impact: Carers can take on a few extra hours of paid work without suddenly losing the whole allowance. But the Lib Dems say it won't start for four years, and losing £1 for every £1 earned is effectively a 100% tax on those extra earnings.

measures.headline: Mayors can charge an overnight 'tourist tax'
measures.detail: Mayors and Strategic Authorities get the power to bring in an Overnight Visitor Levy. Separately, mayors will get 20% of business rates from next year and a share of income tax from 2028, and 100% of business rates will be kept locally by 2030.
measures.impact: Hotel stays in some areas could cost a little more if the local mayor brings in a levy. The money is spent locally.

measures.headline: Defence spending to hit 3% of GDP by 2030
measures.detail: The Defence Investment Plan is fully funded, taking defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030. The OBR estimates that needs an extra £17.3bn in 2029/30. Next year's Spending Review will set out how to reach NATO's 3.5% by 2035. Up to £5bn of investment and lending from the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank will go to defence firms over four years.
measures.impact: A big long-term spending commitment. It's part of why there's little room for tax cuts elsewhere.

measures.headline: Welfare shake-up: face-to-face assessments return
measures.detail: Face-to-face benefit assessments come back. Universal Credit will be rebalanced so it doesn't push people towards being labelled too sick to work. Motability will be reformed, and there's a crackdown on people abroad claiming the UK State Pension 'on the cheap'.
measures.impact: If you claim sickness or disability benefits, expect in-person assessments, and possible changes to how UC treats health conditions and to Motability. Details to come.

measures.headline: First Time Buyer ISA replaces the Lifetime ISA
measures.detail: A new First Time Buyer ISA replaces the Lifetime ISA. From today, the LISA penalty is fixed so buyers whose home costs more than the price limit get back at least what they paid in. From next spring, a new equity loan scheme, 'Your First Home', is backed by £4.7bn of government lending.
measures.impact: If you're saving for a first home in a LISA, you'll no longer lose money if prices push you over the cap. A new Help to Buy-style loan arrives next spring.

measures.headline: £1.5bn more for social and council housing
measures.detail: There's an extra £1.5bn for the Social and Affordable Housing Programme, taking total backing for council housing to £40bn. Cheaper borrowing for councils is extended, land sold to social housing providers will be VAT-free, and biodiversity rules are removed for more brownfield sites.
measures.impact: More council and social homes, faster, especially on brownfield land.

measures.headline: £430m to keep rough sleeper support going every winter
measures.detail: A further £430m keeps the offer to rough sleepers open for the rest of this Parliament, every winter and not just this one.
measures.impact: More emergency accommodation and support for people sleeping rough, guaranteed for several years.

measures.headline: 5p fuel duty cut extended to July
measures.detail: The 5p cut in fuel duty, and the low rate on red diesel, are extended through winter and spring until July.
measures.impact: No rise at the pump from duty for now. That helps drivers, hauliers and farmers. The question returns next summer.

measures.headline: More energy help for lower-income homes
measures.detail: An expansion of the Warm Homes scheme is expected, which helps lower-income households with energy costs and insulation. It could be paid for by the bank levy.
measures.impact: If you're on a lower income, you could get more help with bills or home upgrades this winter. Not mentioned in the speech. We're checking the full Budget documents.

measures.headline: Planned hydrogen levy on gas bills scrapped
measures.detail: The planned Gas Shipper Obligation, a levy to fund hydrogen projects, is dropped. The government will fund those projects directly instead.
measures.impact: One less cost added to household gas bills. Taxpayers pick it up instead.

measures.headline: 25% off electricity bills for 10,000 firms
measures.detail: The British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme will cut electricity bills by 25% for around 10,000 businesses from April, with backdated payments for this year's energy costs.
measures.impact: Big help for energy-heavy manufacturers. Most small businesses won't qualify.

measures.headline: Tax-free side-hustle allowance tripled to £3,000
measures.detail: The trading allowance, the amount you can earn from self-employment or side hustles tax-free, triples from £1,000 to £3,000. A new Young Entrepreneurs Allowance will cover a year of living costs for young founders.
measures.impact: You can earn up to £3,000 a year from selling things, freelancing or a small side business without paying tax on it or having to file for it.

measures.headline: New 'Founders' Relief' on capital gains
measures.detail: Founders of successful companies pay a 10% Capital Gains Tax rate on up to £10m of lifetime gains when they sell. There's also more support for women founders: British Business Bank funds for women-led firms double to £200m, and a new scale-up programme.
measures.impact: Makes building and selling a UK start-up more rewarding. It mostly benefits entrepreneurs with large exits.

measures.headline: Bigger tax break for business investment
measures.detail: The first-year allowance on main-rate assets rises from 40% to 50%, while the ongoing writing-down allowance falls from 14% to 12%.
measures.impact: Firms can deduct more of the cost of new equipment from their taxable profits in the year they buy it. That rewards investing sooner.

measures.headline: Gambling duties up, new tax rules for online sellers
measures.detail: Gambling duties rise to help pay for the Budget. Online sellers and large taxi firms face new sales tax rules. Full details are in the Budget documents.
measures.impact: Betting firms pay more. If you sell online at scale, check how the new rules affect you.

measures.headline: HMRC crackdown and tax admin changes
measures.detail: HMRC gets more funding and stronger powers to collect overdue tax. From 2029, self-assessed income tax will be paid in smaller, more regular payments instead of big lump sums. The rules change on taxing profits taken out of companies, with genuine deals and family business succession protected. There's also a VAT fix for larger taxi firms.
measures.impact: Self-employed people and landlords filing self-assessment will pay little and often from 2029 instead of facing big January bills. Company owners and big taxi operators face tighter rules.

measures.headline: Banks pay an extra 3% surcharge for 15 months
measures.detail: The Bank Surcharge goes up by 3 percentage points, from 3% to 6%, from January for 15 months. The money pays for immediate help with energy bills.
measures.impact: Big banks fund this winter's energy support. Some of the cost could filter through to savings and loan rates.

measures.headline: 70,000 more small firms pay no business rates
measures.detail: For retail, hospitality and leisure businesses, the Small Business Rate Relief threshold rises from £12,000 to £18,000.
measures.impact: 70,000 more shops, cafés, pubs and gyms pay no business rates at all. Half of all shops, restaurants and gyms will now pay none.

measures.headline: £10m duty relief for small brewers and cider makers
measures.detail: About 2,000 small British brewers and cider makers get £10m of alcohol duty relief.
measures.impact: Helps small independent producers, and may soften the effect of the general alcohol duty rise.

measures.headline: Alcohol duty to rise with inflation (about 2p a pint)
measures.detail: Reports suggest alcohol duty will go up in line with RPI inflation (3.9%), which works out at about 2p on a pint of beer.
measures.impact: A small rise at the bar and in shops. Pubs say it adds to their costs. Not mentioned in the speech. We're checking the full Budget documents.

measures.headline: Tax on rental profits could rise by 2 points
measures.detail: Pre-Budget reporting suggests a 2 percentage point rise in the tax on rental income from 2027/28.
measures.impact: Landlords would pay more tax on rental profits. Some of the cost could be passed on to tenants. Not mentioned in the speech. We're checking the full Budget documents.

updates.title: Councils: still struggling
updates.body: The Local Government Association welcomed the money for rough sleeping and social housing, but warned that with no overall rise in council funding, councils will keep struggling to meet demand.

updates.title: Tax-free allowance stays frozen
updates.body: No rise in the £12,570 personal allowance was announced, so the freeze, in place since 2021 and due to last until 2031, continues. The IFS had put the cost of unfreezing it at £6.7bn–£8.4bn a year.

updates.title: 'Wasting another year' on defence, says Lib Dem MP
updates.body: Mike Martin, who chairs the cross-party rearmament group, says putting off a decision on reaching 3.5% leaves Britain 'sleepwalking into a conflict with Russia'.

updates.title: Motor industry: nothing for mechanics' skills
updates.body: The Institute of the Motor Industry says the Budget does nothing meaningful about workforce shortages in vehicle repair. Small firms, which make up over 95% of the sector, need help to take on apprentices.

updates.title: £100 payment will 'barely dent' January's rise, say campaigners
updates.body: The typical bill under the price cap is £1,723 after October's 3.6% rise, and another rise of around 22% is forecast for January. The End Fuel Poverty Coalition says Healey 'talked the talk' but didn't deliver. Citizens Advice warns of another difficult winter.

updates.title: Markets eye a tougher 2027
updates.body: With growth forecast at just 1% next year and inflation still high, CMC Markets says the smaller £15bn buffer matters more, and investors fear a difficult year ahead.

updates.title: OBR: borrowing revised up by nearly £18bn
updates.body: The OBR now expects borrowing of £133.2bn this year (2026/27), up from £115.5bn in March, and higher in every year to 2030/31. It blames higher debt interest, the Budget's own policies, and more spending on welfare and public sector pensions.

updates.title: Experts split on the bank tax
updates.body: Wealth Club's Susannah Streeter says doubling the bank surcharge from 3% to 6% for 15 months 'sends precisely the wrong message' and adds uncertainty.

updates.title: Badenoch: inflation 'eating away' at living standards
updates.body: The Tory leader says it's still easier to live on benefits than to work, and that the Budget does nothing on youth unemployment.

updates.title: Gambling duties and online sellers
updates.body: The round-up confirms higher gambling duties and new sales tax rules for online sellers and large taxi firms, alongside the bank surcharge.

updates.title: A 56-minute speech
updates.body: Shorter than Rachel Reeves' last two Budgets, which ran 77 and 64 minutes.

updates.title: Badenoch: 'a hospital pass'
updates.body: The Conservative leader compares Healey's inheritance to a rugby 'hospital pass' and says you can't have social security without national security.

updates.title: Badenoch: 'Is that it?'
updates.body: Kemi Badenoch says most people will ask 'is that it?', calling it the same story of more borrowing, more taxes and more benefit spending.

updates.title: Lib Dems: rural households left out
updates.body: Tim Farron welcomed the energy help and the paternity pay for the self-employed, but said off-grid homes on heating oil get no cap and the rural fuel duty scheme isn't extended. He added that the Budget gives few clues on how it's paid for.

updates.title: 'Breathing space': 13 mentions
updates.body: Healey used his catchphrase 13 times in the hour-long speech, on energy payments, brewers' relief and his decision to hold an early Budget.

updates.title: Greens question the fiscal rules
updates.body: Green leader Zack Polanski asked whether the fiscal rules Healey praised are the same ever-changing rules that have held back the investment the country needs.

updates.title: Speech over: 'banks will give families breathing space'
updates.body: Healey wrapped up by calling it a Budget for workers, sole traders and parents: revenue raised from those who can afford it, no tax rises on wages or dividends, and tax cuts for millions of families and businesses. Next: Kemi Badenoch's reply, then the OBR at 14:30.

updates.title: Lifetime ISA replaced, new 'Your First Home' loans
updates.body: A First Time Buyer ISA replaces the Lifetime ISA, and the LISA penalty is fixed from today. A £4.7bn equity loan scheme, 'Your First Home', starts next spring.

updates.title: Council housing boost
updates.body: An extra £1.5bn for social and affordable homes, taking the total to £40bn. Cheaper council borrowing, VAT-free land sales to social landlords, and fewer biodiversity rules on brownfield sites.

updates.title: £430m for rough sleeping, every winter
updates.body: Healey commits a further £430m to keep the rough sleeping offer open for the rest of the Parliament.

updates.title: Up to £5bn to back defence firms
updates.body: There will be a new Innovative Defence Finance Taskforce and treaty talks with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands on joint defence funding. The National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank will put up to £5bn into defence over four years.

updates.title: Plan for NATO's 3.5% target coming next year
updates.body: Healey says the defence budget is £14bn higher than in the Conservatives' last year. Next year's Spending Review will show how the UK reaches NATO's 3.5% of GDP by 2035. Earlier, a Tory MP was rebuked by the Deputy Speaker for interrupting.

updates.title: £10bn more support for Ukraine
updates.body: The £10bn of extra economic and military support is mainly loans and export finance guarantees, plus £500m in urgent military funding this winter. Healey says Zelenskyy told them 'you've made my day'.

updates.title: Welfare bill to come down 'in a Labour way'
updates.body: Healey says he won't write off a million young people out of work or leave disabled people in a system 'not fit for purpose', but taxpayers shouldn't fund a failing system for decades.

updates.title: Face-to-face benefit assessments return
updates.body: Universal Credit will be rebalanced so it doesn't push people to sign off as too sick to work. Motability will be reformed, and there's a crackdown on overseas State Pension claims.

updates.title: £100m Local Apprenticeship Service
updates.body: Funded from savings on welfare fraud and error, as part of cutting duplication between central and local government.

updates.title: Defence to reach 3% of GDP by 2030
updates.body: Healey fully funds the Defence Investment Plan. The OBR says hitting 3% needs an extra £17.3bn in 2029/30.

updates.title: AI to save £600m in Whitehall
updates.body: AI in the civil service is expected to save £600m in back-office costs. There's also a review of NHS productivity and AI to free staff from admin.

updates.title: New Misogyny Prevention Fund
updates.body: Healey says work to halve violence against women and girls will speed up, with a new fund run in partnership with the private sector.

updates.title: 'Labour is the party of public services'
updates.body: Healey says day-to-day spending is up more than £40bn a year since 2024, with £37bn more for health next year than in the Conservatives' last year.

updates.title: Tourist tax powers and tax devolution for mayors
updates.body: Mayors can introduce an overnight visitor levy. They'll get 20% of business rates from next year and a share of income tax from 2028, with 100% of business rates kept locally by 2030. Healey calls it 'the most radical act of decentralisation in a generation'.

updates.title: £1.5bn more for regional mayors
updates.body: Mayoral authorities get £1.5bn in flexible loans and new 'Good Growth Funds'. Named projects include the Black Country Metro extension, Gateshead Quayside regeneration and reopening Doncaster Airport.

updates.title: Money for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
updates.body: Wales: £30m for Cardiff Parkway station, £11m for Aberavon Bridge and £2.5m for a North Wales science park. Scotland: £18m for chip design at Edinburgh University and £6m for Glasgow's SEC. Northern Ireland: £7.5m for AI and cyber in Belfast.

updates.title: Regional projects across England
updates.body: They include £20m to restore Liverpool's Littlewoods Building, £15m for Leeds College of Building, £10m each for Bristol Temple Quarter, Stafford market hall and Bury market, and £3m for Plymouth defence skills. Next spring's International Investment Summit will be held in Gateshead.

updates.title: 10% 'Founders' Relief' on up to £10m
updates.body: A new Capital Gains Tax relief lets founders of successful firms pay 10% on up to £10m of lifetime gains.

updates.title: Side-hustle allowance tripled to £3,000
updates.body: The tax-free trading allowance goes from £1,000 to £3,000. There's a Young Entrepreneurs Allowance covering a year's living costs, £200m for women-led businesses, and visa and non-compete reforms so staff can move between start-ups more easily.

updates.title: Self-assessment: pay little and often
updates.body: From 2029, self-assessed income tax will be collected in smaller, regular payments instead of big bills.

updates.title: 'British Data Centre Covenant'
updates.body: Sensitive data such as NHS records will stay in UK data centres. In return for investing locally, creating jobs and protecting water supplies, data centres get faster grid connections.

updates.title: £640m for AI
updates.body: An extra £500m goes to AI safety and security, and £140m to the Sovereign AI Unit to invest in British AI firms.

updates.title: Hydrogen levy on gas bills dropped
updates.body: The planned levy to fund hydrogen through gas bills is scrapped. The government will fund it directly.

updates.title: 'Buy British' push in government contracts
updates.body: Government will do more 'challenge-led' buying so it can be the first customer for innovative firms. A new definition of a UK supplier will favour companies that genuinely invest and create jobs here.

updates.title: £3.5bn of investment announced
updates.body: Over £1bn of life sciences investment from Kindeva, Vertex and Convatec, backed by about £70m of public money, supports 1,000+ jobs. Rolls-Royce will develop next-generation turbine engines in the UK, a £2.5bn investment across the Midlands and Bristol.

updates.title: Banks pay an extra 3% to fund energy help
updates.body: The Bank Surcharge rises by 3 points from January for 15 months, paying for immediate support with energy bills.

updates.title: Cash ISA stays at £20,000, plus a new 'Starter ISA'
updates.body: Healey confirms the cash ISA cut is reversed. A new Starter ISA for first-time investors is on the way.

updates.title: Tax break for business investment
updates.body: The first-year allowance on business assets rises from 40% to 50%, and the writing-down allowance falls from 14% to 12%.

updates.title: HMRC gets more teeth
updates.body: More money and powers for HMRC to chase overdue tax, self-assessment reform from 2029, and new rules on taxing profits taken out of companies.

updates.title: £10m relief for small brewers
updates.body: About 2,000 small brewers and cider makers get £10m in alcohol duty relief.

updates.title: Business rates scrapped for 70,000 more small firms
updates.body: The small business rates relief threshold for shops, hospitality and leisure rises from £12,000 to £18,000. Half of shops, restaurants and gyms will now pay no business rates.

updates.title: Paid paternity leave for the self-employed
updates.body: For the first time, self-employed fathers and partners will be eligible for paid parental leave. Healey calls it a 'downpayment'.

updates.title: Minimum wage up 3.9%
updates.body: The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage both rise by 3.9%, covering 2.3 million low-paid workers.

updates.title: No income tax for pensioners on the State Pension
updates.body: A new Pension Tax Allowance means pensioners with income up to the full new State Pension won't pay income tax this Parliament. Ex-miners get the full pension fund surplus.

updates.title: Fuel duty cut extended to July
updates.body: The 5p fuel duty cut and the low red diesel rate are extended to July because of high fuel prices. The higher mileage rate goes from 25p to 35p a mile.

updates.title: Tariffs suspended on 100+ supermarket items
updates.body: Confirmed in the speech, to help keep the weekly shop down.

updates.title: £100 energy payment for 20 million homes
updates.body: Households in council tax bands A–D get £100 paid directly into their bank accounts this winter to help with energy bills, at a cost of £2.6bn.

updates.title: Confirmed: gas standing charges scrapped
updates.body: Healey confirmed Ofgem will remove gas standing charges, which cost over £100 a year whatever you use, from next year. Electricity is to follow.

updates.title: Electricity VAT cut extended, worth £50
updates.body: The VAT cut on electricity is extended through winter and spring to July, taking about £50 off the annual price cap. Around 10,000 businesses get 25% off electricity from April.

updates.title: Energy shake-up to cut bills
updates.body: New clean power projects will only go ahead if they lower bills. More existing renewables move onto fixed-price contracts to shield bills from gas prices, and grid connections get faster through GB Grid.

updates.title: Cheaper energy is 'top priority'
updates.body: Healey says cheaper energy is the government's top priority, with clean power central to it. Net Zero by 2050 stays.

updates.title: 'Radical reform' of energy promised
updates.body: Healey points to approval of the Jackdaw gas field, which protects hundreds of jobs and is worth an estimated £2.9bn, and a new Energy Wealth Fund for the UK.

updates.title: Growth forecast upgraded
updates.body: The OBR now expects growth of 1.2% this year and 1% next year, then 1.6% in 2028, 1.8% in 2029, 1.7% in 2030 and 1.6% in 2031.

updates.title: Swipe at Liz Truss
updates.body: Healey said the last time the IMF singled out the UK was when Truss 'crashed the economy'. This time, he said, the IMF projects the UK's deficit will be the lowest in the G7 by 2029.

updates.title: OBR forecasts: borrowing falling, debt flat
updates.body: Borrowing is forecast at 4.2% of GDP this year, falling to 3.4% next year, 2.1% in 2029/30 and 1.8% by 2031/32. Debt hovers around 83–84% of GDP before easing to 81.7% by 2031/32.

updates.title: Headroom of £15bn, and no 'broad-based' tax rises
updates.body: Healey ruled out broad tax rises and deep cuts to public services. The OBR puts his buffer against the fiscal rules at £15bn in 2029/30, rising to £22bn in 2030/31. He says the day-to-day deficit will be gone within three years.

updates.title: Rowdy Commons
updates.body: Deputy Speaker Nusrat Ghani called for order twice in seven minutes as opposition MPs jeered.

updates.title: Middle East war has pushed inflation back up
updates.body: The OBR says the Middle East conflict is a key driver of its forecasts. Oil has gone from about $70 to well over $100 a barrel, and gas prices have nearly tripled since February. Inflation, which was due to fall to 2% this year, has risen again as a result.

updates.title: 'Fiscal discipline is my first commitment'
updates.body: Healey says the Budget meets both fiscal rules: day-to-day spending is covered by taxes, and debt falls as a share of the economy. He wants to keep cutting borrowing so less goes on debt interest.

updates.title: Tribute to Reeves, and a Gogglebox joke
updates.body: Healey praised Rachel Reeves, Britain's first female Chancellor, for fiscal discipline and cutting NHS waiting lists. He joked that he'd hoped to be the most-watched minister this week, until the PM turned up on Gogglebox.

updates.title: Three priorities: costs, business, and public services
updates.body: Healey's priorities are 'breathing space' on household and business costs, backing British firms to grow, and action on energy, national security, public services and housing. He says the Budget offers 'fresh hope' and ties it to a 10-Year Plan and next year's Spending Review.

updates.title: 'A Budget for the working people of Britain'
updates.body: Healey opens by calling this a Budget for working people and businesses of all sizes, built on fiscal discipline.

updates.title: Healey is on his feet
updates.body: The Chancellor has stood up at the dispatch box to begin his first Budget speech.

updates.title: Borrowing is running above forecast
updates.body: The government borrowed £24.5bn last month, more than expected. That takes borrowing so far this financial year to £97.8bn, about £6bn above the OBR's forecast, which leaves Healey little room for giveaways.

updates.title: Lib Dems: carers' fix is too slow and too harsh
updates.body: Ed Davey welcomed the end of the Carer's Allowance cliff edge but said it won't take effect for four years. Taking back £1 for every £1 earned amounts to a '100% tax rate' for working carers, he said.

updates.title: PMQs underway before the Budget
updates.body: Andy Burnham opened Prime Minister's Questions at 12:04. Kemi Badenoch pressed him on the EU, and Burnham said there's 'no confusion': Labour's red lines, including no return to free movement, stay for this Parliament. The Budget speech follows straight after.

updates.title: Energy help could be funded by the banks
updates.body: Healey has promised 'breathing space' on costs. More support for lower-income homes through the Warm Homes scheme is tipped, possibly paid for by the bank levy. Tax changes are also expected.

updates.title: Red box out on the steps of No 11
updates.body: Healey posed with the red Budget box outside Downing Street and is heading to the Commons for his first Budget speech.

updates.title: Five 'everyday fixes' already announced
updates.body: Ahead of the speech, the government confirmed: a taper replacing the Carer's Allowance cliff edge, tariffs dropped on 100+ supermarket items (about £21 a year per family), higher tax-free mileage rates, paternity pay for the self-employed (up to £194 a week for two weeks), and 1,000 Post Office drop boxes. Healey admits they 'are not going to change the world'.

updates.title: Bank tax to rise, but temporarily
updates.body: Bloomberg reports Healey will temporarily raise the bank surcharge from its current 3%, but keep it below 8%. Lloyds, Barclays and NatWest shares rose at least 2% on relief that it isn't higher.

updates.title: Drivers watch fuel duty
updates.body: The 5p fuel duty cut is due to start ending in January. Healey wouldn't say beforehand whether he'll delay the rise, and motoring groups are pushing for a further cut.

updates.title: Fewer firms are exporting
updates.body: Among businesses turning over at least £500,000, the share that have ever exported fell from 45% in 2021 to 35% in 2025, according to a government survey. Expect growth and trade to feature in the speech.

updates.title: Who is John Healey?
updates.body: Healey, Labour MP for Rawmarsh and Conisbrough, became Chancellor on 20 July 2026, taking over from Rachel Reeves. Today is his first Budget in the job.

updates.title: The debt backdrop
updates.body: With national debt around £3 trillion, the UK now spends more on debt interest than on defence, schools and prisons combined. Commentators want to see how Healey funds NATO targets of 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

updates.title: Today's timetable, and more expected measures
updates.body: After PMQs, Healey speaks at 12:30. Kemi Badenoch replies for the Conservatives at around 13:30, and the OBR gives its press conference on the forecasts at 14:30. Also tipped: a minimum wage rise, an end to the carers' earnings 'cliff edge', and £432m for rough sleeping.

updates.title: What's already ruled out, and what to watch for
updates.body: Healey has ruled out higher rates of income tax, employee National Insurance and VAT. The big questions for 12:30 are whether the £12,570 tax-free allowance, frozen since 2021, finally goes up, and whether VAT comes off electricity bills.

updates.title: Martin Lewis: most will pay less, but not everyone
updates.body: The money expert welcomed scrapping the gas standing charge, currently about £108 a year. He estimates around 60% of households will pay less and 40% more, as the cost moves into the price per unit. He also warned that the January price cap could rise by around 27%.

updates.title: Alcohol duty expected to rise with inflation
updates.body: Reports say alcohol duty will go up in line with RPI inflation (3.9%), adding about 2p to a pint. Pub groups warn this adds pressure on struggling venues.

updates.title: Business owners call for 'courage'
updates.body: A London bakery founder says rising minimum wage costs are putting firms off taking on trainees and apprentices, and wants the Chancellor to be bolder.

updates.title: Greens: scrapping standing charges is 'tinkering'
updates.body: The Green Party says the gas standing charge move doesn't go far enough on the cost of living.

updates.title: Fuel poverty campaigners welcome the move, with caveats
updates.body: The End Fuel Poverty Coalition calls it 'real relief' for many households but warns that some won't see savings.

updates.title: Gas standing charges to be scrapped
updates.body: The Treasury confirms standing charges on household gas bills will be removed from 2027, or as soon as possible after.

updates.title: Cash ISA cut dropped
updates.body: John Healey has scrapped Rachel Reeves's plan to cut the cash ISA limit to £12,000 for under-65s. The limit stays at £20,000.

updates.title: Expect a cautious Budget
updates.body: Room for manoeuvre is tight because of high debt costs and talk of a possible December election. Most commentators expect few big surprises.

updates.title: It's Budget Day
updates.body: The Chancellor's first priority is expected to be reassuring bond markets. The speech is due around 12:30.
